$comment: Source of truth for every visual value in WorldQuest. Structure and hues come from docs/design/assets/mockup-v1.png; the interaction language — chunky faces sitting on a solid edge that presses down, one heavy rounded typeface everywhere, saturated accents that mean exactly one thing — is modelled on Duolingo, which is the bar this product is being measured against. Components import the SEMANTIC layer only; a raw palette name in a component is a CI failure, because it is what makes theming, high-contrast mode and seasonal event themes possible. Spec: docs/design/design-system.md

palette.$comment: Accent ramps are derived from Duolingo's published accents, then darkened until white sits at ≥3.15:1 on the step that CARRIES A LABEL. Duolingo's own #58CC02 is 2.09:1 against white — it works on their white canvas, where the button reads as one bright object, and it does not work on ours. So the bright original survives as the *400 step and is used where nothing sits on top of it: progress fills, glows, the top sheen of a button face. Nothing in this file is a guess; see the derivation in docs/design/design-system.md §2.

border.$comment: `strong` is a NEUTRAL slate, not a blue. It has to clear 3:1 against the canvas to work as a visible edge, and the first version that did was a saturated blue — which made every idle answer option look selected, because blue is the selection colour three lines below. Luminance is the requirement; hue is a free choice, and the free choice has to be the one that means nothing.

action.$comment: Every accent that carries a label ships as a face/edge pair. The edge is the solid block the face sits on — the thing that makes a button look pressable rather than painted — and it is a real colour, never an opacity of the face, because a translucent edge over a card reads as a smudge.

option.$comment: The answer option is the most-tapped surface in the product, so its states are named here rather than assembled from bg + feedback at each call site.

feedback.$comment: wrong is a muted surface, never red — we state the truth, we do not punish

text.$comment: tertiary is large-text only — the contrast check enforces the floor

depth.$comment: How thick the solid edge under a pressable face is. Not spacing — it is the entire reason a control reads as a physical object, and a control whose edge is 1px reads as a border instead. `press` is how far the face travels on tap; it equals `button` so the face lands flush with the edge's bottom and the object looks compressed rather than moved.

typography.$comment: One typeface, every weight heavy. Duolingo sets its entire interface in a single rounded face (Feather Bold, proprietary) and almost never below semibold — that single decision is most of why it reads as friendly rather than corporate. Nunito is the closest openly-licensed match: rounded terminals, a tall x-height, and a 400–900 range wide enough that hierarchy comes from weight rather than from a second family. Inter and Baloo 2 are gone; two families were fighting each other.

scale.$comment: `hero` sits above `display` for the one-number moments — the XP tally on the lesson summary, and nothing else so far. It exists as a token rather than a local `fontSize: 56` because the rule in this package is that an off-scale literal is a bug; a step the scale genuinely lacked is the case that rule is for. Tabular by default: this number counts up, and proportional digits make the card twitch as it passes 9 → 10.
scale.$comment:button: 17/800 is the iOS button, and the two properties that are NOT here are the point. This step used to be uppercase with +0.6 tracking — the shape of a label you hit rather than read, and the right call for the reference product, whose buttons are set that way on a white canvas. On a dark navy iOS screen it is the loudest non-native thing in the app: iOS has never uppercased a button label, so NÄSTA / HOPPA ÖVER / FORTSÄTT read as a game or an Android port before a user has read a word of them. Sentence case at 17/800 with tracking at zero is the platform's own button. `overline` keeps its uppercase and its tracking — that one matches iOS, which does set grouped-list section headers exactly that way.

motion.$comment: `press` is its own step because it is the shortest thing in the system and the one users feel most often — a button face travelling 4px must land instantly or the control feels soft.

reducedMotion.$comment: springs become fades, Lottie shows its static end frame

layout.$comment:maxContentWidth: How wide a column of content is ever allowed to get. Equal to the `lg` breakpoint on purpose rather than by coincidence: `lg` is already this design system's statement of where a phone layout stops being one, so the cap is that same decision applied instead of a second number to keep in step. Above it the content centres and the margins grow. Without it a 768pt tablet rendered the phone layout stretched — a full-width primary button and 280pt of dead space under the last card, which reads as unfinished rather than spacious. NOTE, because it will be asked: Home still does not fill a 13-inch screen vertically, and that is content rather than layout. Quests and Explore fill it at the same width. Home has four blocks and two of them — Friends and League — are placeholders for features that do not exist yet (v1.5 and v2.0, and HomeScreen says so where it draws them). Building a tablet-specific arrangement to fill space that real content will fill is building around a temporary state, which PROJECT.md names as the most expensive mistake available.
